explanations.explanation: The high priest asks Stephen, “Are these charges true?” No small talk, no warm-up, just a question you could answer with one word. Hold onto that, because Stephen has a whole lot more than one word coming. The question was about the charges, and that's all it was.

explanations.answer: Who gave him the right to teach
explanations.explanation: That's a fair question to ask somebody, but it isn't the one in the text. The high priest asks Stephen, “Are these charges true?” He's pointing right back at what the false witnesses just said. Nobody in this verse asks Stephen for his credentials.

Sounds like something a nosy neighbor would ask, but nobody asks it here. The high priest keeps it short: “Are these charges true?” The whole room just heard the accusations, so he wants an answer to them. Stephen's answer is going to take a while.

Abraham is right, friend. Stephen says, “The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran…” Abraham is the man Stephen calls “our father.” Starting here is like opening a family reunion speech with the great-great-grandparents.

Noah, who built the ark (Genesis 6:22), is a good name, but Stephen doesn't use it here. He says the God of glory appeared to “…our father Abraham…” Stephen is also placing him in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran. Noah never comes up in this speech.

Adam, the first man (Genesis 2:7), would be going back even further than Stephen does, and Stephen is already going back pretty far. The text says the God of glory appeared to “…our father Abraham…” That was while Abraham was still in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran. Adam isn't named in this speech.

Descendants is right. Stephen says God promised to give possession of the land “…to Abraham and his descendants…” So the promise reaches past Abraham to the people who would come after him. Meanwhile, Abraham himself has no inheritance there, not even a foot of ground.

Child is it, baker. God made the promise “…even though he did not yet have a child.” So Abraham is holding a promise about a whole line of descendants with no baby in the picture yet. That's a big promise to carry around with an empty nursery.

Servants isn't in the verse. The text says God promised the land to Abraham and his descendants. Stephen is talking about the people who would come from Abraham himself. Servants don't show up at all.
Wife isn't what the verse says. It says Abraham “…did not yet have a child.” That's the missing piece Stephen points to. The promise was about descendants, and no child had come yet.

Money isn't in this part of the speech. Stephen says God gave Abraham “…no inheritance here, not even a foot of ground.” and then promised the land to Abraham and his descendants. The one time Stephen mentions silver is later, for a tomb Abraham bought (Acts 7:16). What Abraham was missing here was a child.

explanations.answer: In the land He brought Abraham to
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. God says the descendants “…will come forth and worship Me in this place.” Back in verse 4, Stephen said God brought Abraham “…into this land where you are now living.” So the worship is promised for the very land the council is standing in.

explanations.answer: In the land where they were slaves
explanations.explanation: Not quite. God says the descendants would be enslaved and mistreated in that strange land, and that He would punish the nation enslaving them. Then comes the promise: “…afterward they will come forth and worship Me in this place.” They come forth out of the slavery first, and the worship happens in this place, the land Abraham was brought to.

explanations.answer: In the land Abraham left behind
explanations.explanation: That's a sneaky one, but no. Abraham left the land of the Chaldeans (Acts 7:4), but that isn't where God says they will worship. God says they “…will come forth and worship Me in this place.” That place is the land God brought Abraham into.

explanations.answer: Because they were jealous of him
explanations.explanation: Jealousy is right. Stephen says, “Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt.” The twelve patriarchs come from Jacob, and the ones jealous of Joseph are his brothers. And Stephen adds right away, “But God was with him”

Stephen doesn't mention money as the reason. He says the patriarchs sold Joseph “Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph…” The reason Stephen gives is jealousy. Then he says, “But God was with him” and that's the part that matters most.

explanations.answer: Because their father told them to
explanations.explanation: The text says nothing like that. Stephen gives the reason himself: “Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt.” That's the brothers' own jealousy. Stephen doesn't mention their father in the sale.

explanations.answer: Ruler over Egypt and his household
explanations.explanation: Yes, ruler over Egypt and all his household. Stephen says God gave Joseph favor and wisdom in Pharaoh's sight, and Pharaoh “…appointed him ruler over Egypt and all his household.” Think about that climb. Sold as a slave, then running the whole country, and Stephen says it was because God was with him.

That's a big title, but it's not in the text. Stephen says Pharaoh appointed Joseph “…ruler over Egypt and all his household.” That covers a lot more than one army. Nothing here says Joseph led any soldiers.

Chief baker sounds like a dream job to me, I'll admit. But Stephen says Pharaoh made Joseph “…ruler over Egypt and all his household.” That's a far bigger job than running the palace kitchen. Joseph got there because God rescued him from all his troubles and gave him favor and wisdom.

The first part is right, but the king part isn't. Stephen says this king “…knew nothing of Joseph…” and he “…exploited our people and oppressed our fathers…” He even forced them “…to abandon their infants so they would die.” So he was anything but kind, and that makes this one heavy.

False is right, friend. Stephen says the new king “…knew nothing of Joseph…” and he “…exploited our people and oppressed our fathers…” He forced them to abandon their infants so they would die. That's a hard thing to hear, so it's worth pausing on.

Deliver is right. Stephen says Moses “…assumed his brothers would understand that God was using him to deliver them, but they did not.” Moses had a whole picture in his head and nobody else had seen it yet. It's like walking into the room sure everybody got the memo, and nobody got the memo.

Punish isn't the word. Stephen says Moses assumed they would understand that God was using him “…to deliver them…” His people were the ones being mistreated, so this was about rescuing them. God did say He would punish the nation that enslaves them (Acts 7:7), but that's not what Moses assumes here.

Not quite. The text says Moses assumed his brothers would understand that God was using him “…to deliver them, but they did not.” Nobody in the verse is giving a test. It's about rescuing the people who were being mistreated.

Midian is right. Stephen says, “At this remark, Moses fled to the land of Midian, where he lived as a foreigner and had two sons.” That remark had two parts: who made Moses ruler and judge, and whether he wanted to kill the man like he killed the Egyptian. That's a long way to travel because of a comment.
Moab sounds right, but it's not the one Stephen names. He says Moses “…fled to the land of Midian…” That's where he lived as a foreigner and had two sons. Moab isn't in this part of the speech.
Edom isn't the place here. Stephen says Moses fled to the land of Midian after the man pushed him aside. He lived there as a foreigner and had two sons. Edom doesn't come up in this speech.

Redeemer is right. Stephen says God sent Moses “…to be their ruler and redeemer through the angel who appeared to him in the bush.” The man asked who made Moses ruler and judge, and Stephen's answer is that God sent him. The same Moses they pushed aside is the one God sent to them.

Scribe isn't the word, baker. Stephen says God sent Moses “…to be their ruler and redeemer…” Those two titles answer the question the man asked, “Who made you ruler and judge…” Stephen's point is that God sent him.

Commander has a nice ring to it, but it's not in the verse. Stephen says God sent Moses to be “…their ruler and redeemer…” The man had asked who made him ruler and judge. Stephen says God sent him as ruler and redeemer.

Like Moses is right. Stephen says, “This is the same Moses who told the Israelites, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers.’” So Moses is the one speaking, and he says the prophet will be like him. Stephen puts that line right in the middle of his speech about Moses.

Abraham is the first man Stephen talks about, but he isn't the answer here. Moses is the one speaking, and he says, “God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers.” The “me” is Moses. So the prophet is like Moses.

Joseph is the one who gets rescued and rises to power earlier in the speech, but he's not the answer. Stephen says Moses told the Israelites, “God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers.” Who is the “me”? Moses himself. So the answer is Moses.

Obey is right. Stephen says, “…our fathers refused to obey him. Instead, they rejected him and in their hearts turned back to Egypt.” Moses received living words to pass on, and the fathers refused to obey him. That's a big gap between what they were given and what they did.
Crown isn't the word, friend. Stephen says the fathers “…refused to obey him.” They rejected Moses and in their hearts turned back to Egypt. Nobody is talking about a crown here.

Anoint doesn't fit this verse. Stephen says Moses received living words to pass on, “But our fathers refused to obey him.” They rejected him and in their hearts turned back to Egypt. Obey is the word.

Exile beyond Babylon is right. In the quote from the book of the prophets, God says, “Therefore I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.” Stephen is quoting about the idols they made to worship. It's a heavy line, and Stephen doesn't soften it.

Egypt is on their minds, since in their hearts they turned back to Egypt (Acts 7:39). But that's not where God says He will send them. The quote says, “Therefore I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.” That's a different place.

explanations.answer: Out to the desert of Midian
explanations.explanation: Midian is where Moses fled and lived as a foreigner earlier in the speech. It isn't where God says the people go in this quote. God says, “Therefore I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.” That's the answer in Stephen's quote from the prophets.
